architectural_implications.observation: Output cost is currently proportional to generated tokens, so bounded answers still cost per token.

architectural_implications.after: A training objective (RLCD) explicitly optimizes calibrated, epistemically honest probabilities.

architectural_implications.observation: Decision-critical classifiers must expose trustworthy confidence for thresholding and routing.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Sam Witteveen
  • Channel: Sam Witteveen
  • Main topic: TypeSafe AI's Jev model, a System One model designed for structured outputs, classification, and function calling without chat interfaces.
  • Purpose: To analyze and demonstrate Jev by TypeSafe AI, explore its underlying mechanics (RLCD, parallel sampler), compare it to existing LLMs, and walk through practical applications and pricing. Frontier AI labs have focused heavily on reasoning, long chains of thought, and thinking budgets (System 2 thinking), which make models slow, expensive, and opaque for software integration. Software typically needs fast, structured decisions like classification (pick from a list, scoring, yes/no probabilities). TypeSafe AI, founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida (lead author of InstructGPT), spent two years in stealth building Jev, a System One model that outputs typed choices, scores, and probabilities without chat interfaces, token-by-token generation, or hallucination of schema, offering high speed and very low cost.

Topic Map

The State of Frontier Labs and System 2 Reasoning

  • Explanation: Over the past two years, every frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Meta, Qwen) has focused on reasoning using longer chains of thought and thinking budgets. While powerful, these models are slow, expensive, and hide their chain of thought even when billed for it.
  • Key claims:
    • All frontier labs are focused on reasoning and longer chains of thought.
    • Reasoning models are System 2 thinking: slow, deliberate, and effortful.
    • Frontier labs do not let you see the chain of thought even though you pay for it.
  • Examples:
    • Waiting multiple minutes for a reasoning model to return an answer.
  • Terminology:
    • System 1 thinking
    • System 2 thinking
    • Chain of thought
    • Thinking budget
  • Why it matters: Highlights the industry-wide overemphasis on slow reasoning models for tasks that software actually solves with simple classification.

Software Needs System 1 Classification

  • Explanation: Most decisions made inside software every second are not complex System 2 problems; they are simple classification problems (pick-from-a-list, urgency checks, rule violations) that should not take 30 seconds or minutes.
  • Key claims:
    • Most decisions in software are classification problems.
    • Asking reasoning models to return one-word answers wrapped in JSON incurs massive latency and token costs.
  • Examples:
    • Routing a support ticket
    • Checking if a message is spam
    • Escalating to a human
  • Terminology:
    • Classification
    • Latency cost
    • Order-regressive generation
  • Why it matters: Exposes the mismatch between slow chat-based LLMs and the fast, structured decision-making needs of software applications.

Introducing Jev by TypeSafe AI

  • Explanation: TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida (co-author of the InstructGPT paper), came out of stealth with Jev, a model designed for software automation rather than chat.
  • Key claims:
    • Jev has no chat box and does not write left-to-right token by token.
    • Output tokens are free on OpenRouter, while input tokens cost $0.042 per million tokens.
    • Jev is a System One model acting like a typed function call.
  • Examples:
    • Passing unstructured text state and typed questions into jev(state, questions).
  • Terminology:
    • TypeSafe AI
    • Jev
    • Diogo Almeida
    • InstructGPT
    • System One model
  • Why it matters: Introduces a radically different paradigm for integrating AI into software pipelines.

The Three Building Blocks: Choice, Score, and Noul

  • Explanation: Jev operates on three types of questions: Choice (picks one option from a list plus probabilities), Score (rates on a user-defined scale), and Noul (yes/no probability via a sigmoid function).
  • Key claims:
    • There are only three kinds of questions: Choice, Score, and Noul.
    • Outputs contain no text to parse, returning structured probabilities and confidence scores.
    • Jev eliminates faked JSON outputs from order-regressive LLMs.
  • Examples:
    • Classifying support ticket language as French, English, German, or Thai.
    • Scoring customer review sentiment from 0 to 2.
    • Determining whether text is asking a question (Noul).
  • Terminology:
    • Choice
    • Score
    • Noul
    • Sigmoid function
    • Confidence score
  • Why it matters: Provides developers with deterministic, structured primitives instead of parsing fragile text.

Practical Demos: Customer Support, Code Review, Content Moderation, and Agent Tool Selection

  • Explanation: Demonstrating Jev across four practical use cases: customer support routing, code review (SQL injection detection), content moderation, and agent tool selection.
  • Key claims:
    • Jev evaluates inputs rapidly in 300-500ms with extremely low cost.
    • It successfully handles prompt injection, sarcasm, PII detection, and tool selection.
    • Sequential action chains of 20 decisions execute in under 9 seconds for less than 1/20th of a cent.
  • Examples:
    • Routing duplicate charge tickets to Billing with 97% confidence.
    • Detecting SQL injection vulnerabilities in Python code.
    • Playing Doom with 10 queries per second for ~$7/hour.
  • Terminology:
    • Prompt injection
    • PII detection
    • Tool selection
    • Sequential actions
    • Doom gameplay
  • Why it matters: Proves that Jev's architecture handles complex software workflows with high speed, accuracy, and low cost.

How Does It Work? RLCD and Parallel Sampler

  • Explanation: TypeSafe AI utilizes a new model architecture, a parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and a training method called Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).
  • Key claims:
    • RLCD stands for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.
    • Unlike RLHF (Human Preference) and RLVR (Verifiable Rewards), RLCD optimizes for calibrated decisions with epistemically honest probabilities.
    • End-to-end response time is 700ms-500ms (40x-200x faster than frontier models).
  • Examples:
    • Comparing existing LLMs (RLHF, RLVR) with System One + Jev (RLCD).
  • Terminology:
    • RLCD
    • Parallel sampler
    • RLHF
    • RLVR
    • Calibrated decisions
    • Epistemically honest probabilities
  • Why it matters: Explains the technical breakthrough enabling fast, non-autoregressive, calibrated structured outputs.

Key Points

Chat is the wrong interface for software

  • Explanation: Software applications do not want paragraphs of text; they want structured values they can use immediately without parsing latency.
  • Evidence: Traditional LLMs require parsing markdown JSON out of conversational text streams, introducing latency and failure points.
  • Practical implication: Developers should use function-call-like interfaces that return typed values directly.

Jev eliminates token-by-token generation for classification

  • Explanation: Jev does not write text left-to-right; it evaluates the whole answer at once using parallel sampling.
  • Evidence: Output tokens are priced at $0/M on OpenRouter because generation is non-autoregressive for the output values.
  • Practical implication: Massive reduction in latency (700-500ms) and cost.

Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)

  • Explanation: A new training methodology optimized for calibrated, epistemically honest probability scores rather than human conversational preferences.
  • Evidence: Outputs include accurate confidence scores and probability distributions across all available options.
  • Practical implication: Eliminates hallucinations in structured outputs and tool selection.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Jev Function Call Framework

  • How it works: Treats the model call like a typed function taking state and typed questions.
  • Components:
    • State (unstructured text or data)
    • Typed Questions (Choice, Score, Noul)
  • When to use: Whenever software needs fast, structured classification, routing, scoring, or probability checks.

Examples & Case Studies

Passing support ticket text through Jev with Choice, Score, and Noul questions.

  • Illustrates: How Jev classifies text into billing, technical, or account categories with confidence scores.
  • Lesson: Structured building blocks eliminate prompt engineering and fragile JSON parsing.

Jev running 20 sequential decisions to manage an eCommerce order workflow.

  • Illustrates: Chaining multiple classification decisions together efficiently.
  • Lesson: Complex multi-step software agents can run reliably and cheaply using System 1 models.

Jev playing Doom by making 10 queries per second.

  • Illustrates: The extreme speed and real-time capability of Jev's parallel sampling architecture.
  • Lesson: Real-time automated control is viable at a cost of ~$7/hour.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Try Jev on OpenRouter for classification and routing tasks.
    • Replace fragile JSON prompt generation with typed classification blocks.
  • Strategic:
    • System 1 models are unlocking fast software automation that chat-based LLMs were too slow and expensive for.
    • RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions) represents a major shift away from RLHF for functional software.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • What underlying model architecture powers Jev?
    • How well does RLCD scale to larger models or more complex domains outside classification?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Jev output tokens are free on OpenRouter. (pricing)
  • Jev achieves 700ms-500ms end-to-end response time. (performance)
  • Diogo Almeida was a lead author on the InstructGPT paper. (factual)

Notable Quotes

"Every frontier lab... all of it in one direction. They've all been focused on reasoning." (at 0:06) "Chat is the wrong interface for software." (at 4:02) "This is what we were all faking." (at 6:38) "We built a new stack entirely focused on automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)." (at 21:47)

Compressed Summary

  • Frontier labs focus on slow System 2 reasoning models.
  • Software needs fast System 1 classification, not chat paragraphs.
  • TypeSafe AI's Jev model provides typed Choice, Score, and Noul outputs.
  • Trained with RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions).
  • Delivers non-autoregressive structured outputs in 700-500ms with zero hallucination of schema.
  • Keywords: jev, typesafe, rlcd, classification, system1
  • Core insight: Jev replaces slow, conversational, chat-based LLMs with a fast System 1 model optimized via RLCD for deterministic, typed classification and structured software automation.

- **Main topic**: TypeSafe AI's Jev model, a System One model designed for structured outputs, classification, and function calling without chat interfaces.
- **Purpose**: To analyze and demonstrate Jev by TypeSafe AI, explore its underlying mechanics (RLCD, parallel sampler), compare it to existing LLMs, and walk through practical applications and pricing.
Frontier AI labs have focused heavily on reasoning, long chains of thought, and thinking budgets (System 2 thinking), which make models slow, expensive, and opaque for software integration. Software typically needs fast, structured decisions like classification (pick from a list, scoring, yes/no probabilities). TypeSafe AI, founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida (lead author of InstructGPT), spent two years in stealth building Jev, a System One model that outputs typed choices, scores, and probabilities without chat interfaces, token-by-token generation, or hallucination of schema, offering high speed and very low cost.
## Topic Map
### The State of Frontier Labs and System 2 Reasoning
- **Explanation**: Over the past two years, every frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Meta, Qwen) has focused on reasoning using longer chains of thought and thinking budgets. While powerful, these models are slow, expensive, and hide their chain of thought even when billed for it.
- **Key claims**:
  - All frontier labs are focused on reasoning and longer chains of thought.
  - Reasoning models are System 2 thinking: slow, deliberate, and effortful.
  - Frontier labs do not let you see the chain of thought even though you pay for it.
- **Examples**:
  - Waiting multiple minutes for a reasoning model to return an answer.
- **Terminology**:
  - System 1 thinking
  - System 2 thinking
  - Chain of thought
  - Thinking budget
- **Why it matters**: Highlights the industry-wide overemphasis on slow reasoning models for tasks that software actually solves with simple classification.
### Software Needs System 1 Classification
- **Explanation**: Most decisions made inside software every second are not complex System 2 problems; they are simple classification problems (pick-from-a-list, urgency checks, rule violations) that should not take 30 seconds or minutes.
- **Key claims**:
  - Most decisions in software are classification problems.
  - Asking reasoning models to return one-word answers wrapped in JSON incurs massive latency and token costs.
- **Examples**:
  - Routing a support ticket
  - Checking if a message is spam
  - Escalating to a human
- **Terminology**:
  - Classification
  - Latency cost
  - Order-regressive generation
- **Why it matters**: Exposes the mismatch between slow chat-based LLMs and the fast, structured decision-making needs of software applications.
### Introducing Jev by TypeSafe AI
- **Explanation**: TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida (co-author of the InstructGPT paper), came out of stealth with Jev, a model designed for software automation rather than chat.
- **Key claims**:
  - Jev has no chat box and does not write left-to-right token by token.
  - Output tokens are free on OpenRouter, while input tokens cost $0.042 per million tokens.
  - Jev is a System One model acting like a typed function call.
- **Examples**:
  - Passing unstructured text state and typed questions into jev(state, questions).
- **Terminology**:
  - TypeSafe AI
  - Jev
  - Diogo Almeida
  - InstructGPT
  - System One model
- **Why it matters**: Introduces a radically different paradigm for integrating AI into software pipelines.
### The Three Building Blocks: Choice, Score, and Noul
- **Explanation**: Jev operates on three types of questions: Choice (picks one option from a list plus probabilities), Score (rates on a user-defined scale), and Noul (yes/no probability via a sigmoid function).
- **Key claims**:
  - There are only three kinds of questions: Choice, Score, and Noul.
  - Outputs contain no text to parse, returning structured probabilities and confidence scores.
  - Jev eliminates faked JSON outputs from order-regressive LLMs.
- **Examples**:
  - Classifying support ticket language as French, English, German, or Thai.
  - Scoring customer review sentiment from 0 to 2.
  - Determining whether text is asking a question (Noul).
- **Terminology**:
  - Choice
  - Score
  - Noul
  - Sigmoid function
  - Confidence score
- **Why it matters**: Provides developers with deterministic, structured primitives instead of parsing fragile text.
### Practical Demos: Customer Support, Code Review, Content Moderation, and Agent Tool Selection
- **Explanation**: Demonstrating Jev across four practical use cases: customer support routing, code review (SQL injection detection), content moderation, and agent tool selection.
- **Key claims**:
  - Jev evaluates inputs rapidly in 300-500ms with extremely low cost.
  - It successfully handles prompt injection, sarcasm, PII detection, and tool selection.
  - Sequential action chains of 20 decisions execute in under 9 seconds for less than 1/20th of a cent.
- **Examples**:
  - Routing duplicate charge tickets to Billing with 97% confidence.
  - Detecting SQL injection vulnerabilities in Python code.
  - Playing Doom with 10 queries per second for ~$7/hour.
- **Terminology**:
  - Prompt injection
  - PII detection
  - Tool selection
  - Sequential actions
  - Doom gameplay
- **Why it matters**: Proves that Jev's architecture handles complex software workflows with high speed, accuracy, and low cost.
### How Does It Work? RLCD and Parallel Sampler
- **Explanation**: TypeSafe AI utilizes a new model architecture, a parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and a training method called Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).
- **Key claims**:
  - RLCD stands for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.
  - Unlike RLHF (Human Preference) and RLVR (Verifiable Rewards), RLCD optimizes for calibrated decisions with epistemically honest probabilities.
  - End-to-end response time is 700ms-500ms (40x-200x faster than frontier models).
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing existing LLMs (RLHF, RLVR) with System One + Jev (RLCD).
- **Terminology**:
  - RLCD
  - Parallel sampler
  - RLHF
  - RLVR
  - Calibrated decisions
  - Epistemically honest probabilities
- **Why it matters**: Explains the technical breakthrough enabling fast, non-autoregressive, calibrated structured outputs.
## Key Points
### Chat is the wrong interface for software
- **Explanation**: Software applications do not want paragraphs of text; they want structured values they can use immediately without parsing latency.
- **Evidence**: Traditional LLMs require parsing markdown JSON out of conversational text streams, introducing latency and failure points.
- **Practical implication**: Developers should use function-call-like interfaces that return typed values directly.
### Jev eliminates token-by-token generation for classification
- **Explanation**: Jev does not write text left-to-right; it evaluates the whole answer at once using parallel sampling.
- **Evidence**: Output tokens are priced at $0/M on OpenRouter because generation is non-autoregressive for the output values.
- **Practical implication**: Massive reduction in latency (700-500ms) and cost.
### Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)
- **Explanation**: A new training methodology optimized for calibrated, epistemically honest probability scores rather than human conversational preferences.
- **Evidence**: Outputs include accurate confidence scores and probability distributions across all available options.
- **Practical implication**: Eliminates hallucinations in structured outputs and tool selection.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Jev Function Call Framework
- **How it works**: Treats the model call like a typed function taking state and typed questions.
- **Components**:
  - State (unstructured text or data)
  - Typed Questions (Choice, Score, Noul)
- **When to use**: Whenever software needs fast, structured classification, routing, scoring, or probability checks.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Passing support ticket text through Jev with Choice, Score, and Noul questions.
- **Illustrates**: How Jev classifies text into billing, technical, or account categories with confidence scores.
- **Lesson**: Structured building blocks eliminate prompt engineering and fragile JSON parsing.
### Jev running 20 sequential decisions to manage an eCommerce order workflow.
- **Illustrates**: Chaining multiple classification decisions together efficiently.
- **Lesson**: Complex multi-step software agents can run reliably and cheaply using System 1 models.
### Jev playing Doom by making 10 queries per second.
- **Illustrates**: The extreme speed and real-time capability of Jev's parallel sampling architecture.
- **Lesson**: Real-time automated control is viable at a cost of ~$7/hour.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Try Jev on OpenRouter for classification and routing tasks.
  - Replace fragile JSON prompt generation with typed classification blocks.
- **Strategic**:
  - System 1 models are unlocking fast software automation that chat-based LLMs were too slow and expensive for.
  - RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions) represents a major shift away from RLHF for functional software.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - What underlying model architecture powers Jev?
  - How well does RLCD scale to larger models or more complex domains outside classification?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Jev output tokens are free on OpenRouter. (pricing)
- Jev achieves 700ms-500ms end-to-end response time. (performance)
- Diogo Almeida was a lead author on the InstructGPT paper. (factual)
## Notable Quotes
> "Every frontier lab... all of it in one direction. They've all been focused on reasoning." (at 0:06)
> "Chat is the wrong interface for software." (at 4:02)
> "This is what we were all faking." (at 6:38)
> "We built a new stack entirely focused on automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)." (at 21:47)
## Compressed Summary
- Frontier labs focus on slow System 2 reasoning models.
- Software needs fast System 1 classification, not chat paragraphs.
- TypeSafe AI's Jev model provides typed Choice, Score, and Noul outputs.
- Trained with RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions).
- Delivers non-autoregressive structured outputs in 700-500ms with zero hallucination of schema.
- **Keywords**: jev, typesafe, rlcd, classification, system1
- **Core insight**: Jev replaces slow, conversational, chat-based LLMs with a fast System 1 model optimized via RLCD for deterministic, typed classification and structured software automation.
